title: Monolith
summary: A 12-poster series for an experimental music festival, built on one brutalist grid and oversized type.
lede: A poster system where one grid, one typeface and one attitude generate twelve distinct voices.
overview: Nocturne is a three-night festival for experimental music, and its identity had to work as loudly at 3 metres as it did at 30 centimetres. The answer was constraint: a single six-column grid, a single grotesque, and a rule that every poster must break exactly one of the system’s rules.

Each night produced four variations — halftone performance photography, duotone colour fields, pure typographic compositions and one deliberate failure per set. The series was screen-printed in two inks, so every decision had to survive a physical process with no undo button.
quote: A poster should stop you at ten metres and reward you at ten centimetres.

process.d: One six-column grid, two margins, zero exceptions — defined before a single image was chosen.
A single grotesque pushed from 8pt credits to 400pt headlines, tracking tightened as size grew.
Performance photography pushed through halftone, duotone and high-contrast thresholds.
Two-ink screen printing, paper tests and registration marks as part of the visual language.

bts: Twelve dummies were printed on newsprint before the final run. Three compositions died on the wall — too clever at distance — and were rebuilt the same night.

title: Signal
summary: A modular content system of 60+ templates that keeps a fast-moving audio brand unmistakably itself.
lede: Sixty-plus social templates that let a small team publish daily without ever looking generic.
overview: Aether Audio ships a product every six weeks and was publishing with one-off graphics made in a hurry. The system had to make the fast path the beautiful path: modular frames, fixed type roles and a colour logic that survives whatever photo arrives from the studio.

Templates were built for every format — announcements, quotes, carousels, equaliser posts and launch films — then handed over with motion presets so the in-house team could animate without opening a blank composition.
quote: A design system is only real when the fastest way to use it is also the best-looking one.

process.d: Eighteen months of posts sorted into what felt ownable, what felt generic and what was missing.
Frame library with fixed type roles, image ratios and a two-accent colour logic.
After Effects rigs for entrances, equalisers and product callouts, exported as templates.
A compact guide plus working files so the team can ship without a designer in the loop.

bts: The whole system was stress-tested by rebuilding two real campaigns inside it before anything was documented.

title: Ferro
summary: A typographic identity for an architecture studio — custom wordmark, editorial grid, concrete restraint.
lede: An architecture studio described in one weight of type and one honest grid.
overview: Ferro builds in concrete, steel and daylight, and wanted an identity that behaved the same way: structural, unornamented, precise. The wordmark was drawn from a single stroke weight with cut terminals echoing formwork lines.
Around it sits an editorial system — project sheets, proposal covers and site signage — all set on a baseline grid that lets photography carry the emotion while the type simply holds the frame.
quote: Identity for architects should feel like a good elevation: everything on it is structure.

process.d: Custom letterforms drawn at one weight with cut terminals borrowed from formwork.
A baseline grid shared by business cards, proposals and site hoardings.
Project sheets, signage, drawing-title blocks and a lightweight web starter.
A short, image-led document that shows the system instead of describing it.

bts: The final mark was drawn three times — twice too soft. The version that shipped was traced from an actual concrete sample photo.

title: Kinetic Identity
summary: A title sequence and motion language that turns a design conference identity into movement.
lede: A static conference identity taught how to breathe, stretch and cut on beat.
overview: Format’s identity was a set of rigid rectangles. The motion brief was to keep that rigour while making it feel alive — no bouncing, no easing tricks, just geometric behaviour: slide, clip, stack, reveal.
The deliverable was not one film but a language — a title sequence, forty lower-thirds, stage transitions and a set of timing rules so every screen in the venue felt cut by the same editor.
quote: Motion is not decoration applied afterwards; it is the identity seen in time.

process.d: One grid, three speeds, a shared easing curve written down before animation began.
A 40-second opener built entirely from clips of the existing rectangle system.
Lower-thirds, stings and stage wipes as reusable, editable compositions.
Exports tested on LED walls, streams and social crops in parallel.

bts: Everything was animated on a 12fps beat grid first, then smoothed — the chunky pass stayed in the final cut for four shots.

title: Nightshift
summary: A one-take-feel music film cut from four hours of night footage into three minutes of rhythm.
lede: Four hours of handheld night footage, cut until it felt like a single unbroken breath.
overview: The band wanted the feeling of one continuous take without the limits that come with actually shooting one. The edit hides its seams: every cut lands on a light source crossing frame, so the eye never catches the join.
Colour was pulled toward sodium and shadow — amber streetlight against a cold blue base — with grain held rather than cleaned, because the footage’s imperfections were the point.
quote: The best cut is the one the audience feels in their chest before they see it.

process.d: Four hours logged by light, movement and lyric — not by the storyboard.
Structure built to the song’s stems, with transitions hidden inside light wipes.
Sodium amber against cold blue base, grain retained, blacks lifted slightly.
Location ambience layered under the mix so the city never leaves the frame.

bts: Two of the best shots came from the battery dying mid-recording — the camera’s final frames became the opening.

title: Pulse Reels
summary: A vertical-first reel system engineered for sound-off viewing and fast product drops.
lede: Product drops designed for a 3-second decision made without sound.
overview: Rova drops a product every fortnight and needed reels that read instantly with the sound off. The system uses three fixed beats — hook, proof, payoff — with type large enough to survive a thumbnail and timing tight enough to survive a swipe.
Each drop ships as a set: a hero reel, three cutdowns and a still frame pulled from the same timeline, so the campaign stays coherent across feed, stories and paid placements.
quote: In vertical video, the first frame is the headline and the second is the hook.

process.d: Three opening patterns tested against real retention data from the brand account.
Hook, proof, payoff — fixed durations so every drop feels like part of a series.
Oversized kinetic captions carrying the full message with audio muted.
A project template that turns a new drop into eight exports in under an hour.

bts: Shoots are filmed twice as tall as needed so the edit can reframe for stories, feed and paid without a second camera.

title: Obsidian Sky
summary: A four-minute speculative AI film about memory, landscape and the images we lose.
lede: A speculative short film assembled from generated frames, then cut, graded and finished like live action.
overview: Obsidian Sky imagines a landscape that keeps rewriting itself — a place where every return reveals a version of the memory that never happened. The film was built by generating in disciplined bursts: one location, one palette, one camera behaviour per sequence.

Generation was only the raw footage. The real work was editorial — selecting eleven usable frames from hundreds, stabilising motion, rebuilding continuity, grading everything into one cinematic base and adding sound design that gives synthetic images weight.
quote: AI gives you infinite frames; the craft is choosing the eleven that matter.

process.d: Shot list, lens language and palette locked before generation to avoid model drift.
Hundreds of candidates generated, then filtered to a usable selects reel.
Stabilisation, warp repair and re-timing so synthetic shots behave like real footage.
Unified cinematic grade plus designed ambience and a sparse score.

bts: The opening shot exists in nineteen versions. The fourteenth — technically the worst render — is the one that made the film.

title: Chroma Drift
summary: An ongoing study of colour, material and light generated at the edge of legibility.
lede: Colour fields and impossible materials, prompted like photography and finished like painting.
overview: Chroma Drift started as a daily discipline: one image, one material, one light source, every morning for a hundred days. The constraint was to never show the whole object — always the edge, the surface, the moment before recognition.
Raw generations were treated as negatives. Each final frame is a composite of several passes, retouched for banding, grain and colour accuracy so it holds up in print at poster scale.
quote: Generated images get interesting the moment you stop accepting the first result.

process.d: One material, one light, one crop — a hundred mornings, no exceptions.
Camera, lens and stock language instead of adjectives to keep results photographic.
Multi-pass blending for colour accuracy and deliberate chromatic drift.
Grain, banding repair and soft-proofing for poster-scale output.

bts: The failed renders — melted surfaces, broken geometry — became a second series shown alongside the clean ones.

title: Latent Garden
summary: A latent-space walkthrough where botanical forms grow, mutate and dissolve in real time.
lede: An experiment in moving a camera through a space that does not exist.
overview: Latent Garden is a research piece: a continuous camera move through a botanical world that regenerates as it is travelled. Workflows were built in ComfyUI with interpolation between seed clusters so growth and decay read as one unbroken motion.
The final piece mixes generated motion with hand animation — particle overlays, depth holds and a beat-locked edit — to prove that generative footage can be directed rather than merely collected.
quote: Every model has a temperament. The work starts when you learn to negotiate with it.

process.d: Node graphs for interpolation, depth control and seed-to-seed morphing.
Clusters of seeds plotted so movement through space feels intentional.
Hand-drawn overlays, particles and holds added over generated motion.
Beat-locked assembly, noise management and multi-resolution exports.

bts: The render farm was a laptop for three nights. Heat, not creativity, set the production schedule.

title: Dust & Light
summary: A nine-minute documentary inside a third-generation letterpress workshop.
lede: Nine minutes inside a workshop where ink, metal and habit have outlived three generations.
overview: The film follows a single working week: setting type, pulling proofs, arguing about a client’s hyphenation. There is no narration — the machines and the hands carry the story, and the edit holds long enough for the audience to hear a room think.
Light was the structure. Morning shoots used one window and reflectors only; the grade kept warm highlights against cool shadow so dust in the air became visible punctuation between scenes.
quote: Documentary is not about finding the truth on screen; it is about not getting in its way.

process.d: Visits with no camera to learn the room, the routines and where the light falls.
Two-person crew, available light and a single lens choice to stay invisible.
Cut without music first so structure rests on rhythm and natural sound.
Warm highlights, cool shadows, and a soundscape built from the workshop itself.

bts: The press could not be stopped for takes — every shot was recorded against real production sound, which set the entire edit rhythm.

title: Terra Nova
summary: A reforestation campaign connecting posters, film and social into one growing system.
lede: A campaign that grows — one poster, one frame and one seedling at a time.
overview: Verdant plants a forest a hectare at a time and needed a campaign that could grow with the numbers rather than shouting about them once. The system: every published asset adds one mark to a shared grid, and the grid becomes an image of the forest by year’s end.
Film, outdoor posters and social all share the same growth logic, so the campaign reads as a single accelerating gesture across every channel it touches.
quote: A campaign should behave like the thing it is advocating for.

process.d: One mark per asset, accumulating into a shared yearly image.
Documentary-led 60s spot following a single planting season end to end.
Poster series where each execution advances the growth grid.
Templates that let the client publish without breaking the concept.

bts: Half the footage came from volunteers’ phones — reframed, graded and cut alongside the main camera without apology.

title: Set Notes
summary: A behind-the-scenes archive of sets, screens and happy accidents from the last two years.
lede: The making-of record: what the final frame never shows about how it got made.
overview: Set Notes is an ongoing archive kept on every production — c-stands and cable on the floor, prompt screens mid-generation, marked-up print dummies, the coffee that fixed a broken third act.
It exists as an honest counterweight to the polished case studies on this site: proof that premium results come from iteration, mess and a lot of near misses.
quote: Show the process and the work becomes believable; hide it and it becomes suspicious.

process.d: Ten minutes at wrap, every shoot, no exceptions — the archive fills itself.
Frames chosen for process truth rather than how flattering they look.
Sequenced like a diary: project, problem, resolution, residue.
Released as short notes alongside each finished case study.

bts: This archive is the behind-the-scenes section of every project on this site — including the photographs of it being made.
